# Independent judges and judicial review (`independent_judiciary_judicial_review`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: needs rule_of_law; helped by written_constitution
- Core idea: Judges are appointed for life or a long fixed term, paid a salary that cannot be cut, and cannot be removed for the way they decide; they give public reasons. A judge who cannot be punished by the ruler can rule against him. Judicial review goes one step further: a court may refuse to apply an order or statute that contradicts a higher law (constitution, charter). Hamilton's argument: the court is the least dangerous branch because it commands neither army nor treasury, so giving it the last word on legality costs little and protects everyone.
- Pitfalls:
  - Forgetting that a court has no force of its own: its rulings hold only if officials and the army obey, so it needs allies and a habit of compliance
  - Thinking judicial review is written into the US Constitution: the Supreme Court inferred it in Marbury v. Madison (1803)
  - Offering it to a monarch who is himself the highest judge: it removes a core royal power and will be read as an attack
  - Ignoring the opposite failure: irremovable judges can become a closed caste or a political actor, and whoever controls appointments controls the court
- History: greece: c. 415 BC – Athenian graphe paranomon: any citizen may indict a decree as contrary to the laws before a jury court; 403 BC laws ranked above decrees; rome: from 5th c. BC – tribunes may veto magistrates' acts; no court could annul a law; china: from Qin/Han – censors may impeach officials and remonstrate with the emperor; magistrates combined administration and judging and were never independent; islamic: 8th c. onwards – qadis judge by a law the ruler did not make, and stories of caliphs appearing as ordinary litigants set the ideal; in practice rulers appointed, dismissed and bypassed them; europe: 1610 – Coke in Bonham's Case claims common law can control an Act of Parliament (not followed in England); 1701 Act of Settlement gives judges tenure during good behaviour; 1920 Austrian Constitutional Court designed by Kelsen; americas: 1803 – Marbury v. Madison: the US Supreme Court declares a statute void; india: 1950 – Supreme Court with power of review; 1973 it holds that even amendments may not destroy the constitution's basic structure
- Read:
  - Alexander Hamilton, The Federalist No. 78 (1788)
  - Mauro Cappelletti, Judicial Review in the Contemporary World (1971)
